title: Naturalism in the Philosophy of Mathematics

summaries.example: Imagine a class deciding whether a new rule belongs in a math game. One student says, “It feels right.” Another checks whether it works with the rules already used in mathematics and science. A naturalist usually gives more authority to those established methods than to a private feeling. But people can still ask whether mathematics describes real objects, such as numbers, or only patterns and rules.
summaries.summary: This entry explains naturalism in the philosophy of mathematics. Methodological naturalism says that philosophy of mathematics should rely mainly on standards already used successfully in science, mathematics, or both. It often supports keeping established mathematics instead of changing it because of a separate philosophical idea. The entry also describes disagreements within naturalism. Some versions give science the leading role; others give mathematics that role; and a mixed view uses both. A major question is what “authority” means: must we accept whatever these standards support, or should we merely avoid claims that conflict with them? The entry also discusses a view that all things are natural or physical. That view has trouble explaining abstract objects such as numbers and sets, since they do not seem to be located in space or able to cause physical events.
key_ideas: Naturalism asks which methods should guide philosophy of mathematics.
Some naturalists trust science, some trust mathematics, and some trust both.
Naturalism often resists attempts to replace ordinary mathematics with a different system for outside philosophical reasons.
Naturalists still face difficult questions about where science ends, how strong its support must be, and how different standards should be balanced.
Another kind of naturalism says that everything that exists is natural, which can create problems for the idea that abstract mathematical objects exist.
summaries.why_it_matters: Mathematics is used everywhere, but people disagree about what mathematical truths are and how we know them. Naturalism offers one way to connect mathematics with the successful practices of science and mathematicians. Studying it helps us notice that even a familiar subject can raise big questions about evidence, rules, truth, and reality.

important_terms.definition: An approach that gives special authority to the methods and standards of science, mathematics, or both when thinking about mathematics.
The usual rules and ways of checking work inside mathematics, such as proof and careful reasoning.
Ways scientists judge ideas, including how well they fit evidence, explain things, and work simply and successfully.
The view that mathematics should not be changed just because someone outside mathematical practice dislikes it.
The view that mathematical objects, such as numbers or sets, exist independently of people and are not physical objects.

questions_to_think_about: Should a good mathematical proof be accepted even if it has no use in science?
Can a method be useful without proving that its conclusions are true?
Who should decide whether a mathematical idea is acceptable: mathematicians, scientists, philosophers, or all of them?
If numbers are not physical things, how could we know about them?

summaries.example: Consider a proposed new axiom for set theory. A mathematical naturalist may ask whether it fits the aims and methods of current set theory. A scientific naturalist may ask whether accepting it improves the best overall scientific theory, perhaps through simplicity or explanatory value. A mathematical-cum-scientific naturalist must decide how to weigh those considerations if they conflict. A heterogeneous naturalist may treat the axiom as a mathematical matter while using scientific standards to interpret what the resulting theory is about.
summaries.summary: The entry examines naturalism as a family of approaches to the philosophy of mathematics. Methodological naturalism holds that philosophy should recognize the authority of standards developed within natural science, mathematics, or both. The authority claim itself is ambiguous. A strong biconditional version accepts a proposition exactly when the relevant standards sanction it. A weaker compatibility version rejects propositions that conflict with those standards without requiring acceptance of everything they support. The entry explores the boundary problem: neither “science” nor “mathematics” has an obviously sharp, algorithmic definition, and actual practice involves degrees of support rather than simple yes-or-no verdicts. It also evaluates motivations based on current success, agreement, and historical track records, noting that achievement within one field may not establish authority in another. Heterogeneous naturalism, associated especially with Maddy, treats mathematical practice as autonomous in mathematics proper but uses science for philosophical interpretation. The entry questions both the autonomy claim and whether autonomy would by itself make mathematical claims acceptable. Finally, ontological naturalism is considered in relation to platonism, reductionism, structuralism, and the epistemic challenge posed by abstract objects.
key_ideas: Naturalism is better understood as an orientation toward inquiry than as one completely fixed doctrine.
Its authority claim can be interpreted in several strengths: standards may be decisive, overriding, emphasized, or merely treated as constraints.
The anti-revisionist tendency of naturalism does not make every version conservative: scientific naturalism can recommend judging mathematics by a new, external standard.
Arguments from scientific success, agreement, and historical achievement motivate naturalism, but each faces the objection that success in one domain may not establish authority in another.
Heterogeneous naturalism depends on the controversial idea that mathematical practice is methodologically autonomous from philosophy and science.
Ontological and epistemological naturalism raise the problem of how we could know abstract mathematical objects if they are causally isolated from us.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate concerns more than a label for a philosophical position. It asks how standards from successful practices should guide questions about truth, existence, and justification. It also exposes a recurring problem in philosophy: evidence that works well in one area may not automatically settle questions in another. Understanding these distinctions helps separate claims about mathematical practice from claims about what mathematics means or what mathematical objects are.

important_terms.definition: The methodological thesis that authoritative standards in philosophy of mathematics come from natural science, mathematics, or their combination.
The version of methodological naturalism that treats natural-scientific standards as authoritative for philosophy of mathematics.
The version that treats mathematical standards as authoritative both in mathematics and, on some formulations, in its philosophy.
A view combining scientific and mathematical standards, requiring a policy for resolving conflicts between them.
The claim that mathematics proper should follow its own standards while philosophy of mathematics follows scientific standards.
The problem of identifying a non-arbitrary boundary between science, mathematics, philosophy, and other kinds of inquiry.
The position that mathematical objects are abstract entities existing independently of minds and physical space.
The view that all entities are natural, often understood as the claim that only spatiotemporal entities exist.

questions_to_think_about: Is avoiding conflict with science enough to justify a philosophy of mathematics, or should science be allowed to override mathematical practice?
Can a discipline’s success in answering its own questions establish its authority over different questions?
If scientific standards and mathematical standards disagree, what could justify giving one more weight?
Does the fact that mathematicians accept a method show that the method is justified, or only that it is widely used?
Would a mathematical theory be less credible if its truth depended on contingent features of our physical universe?

summaries.example: Suppose your school is choosing rules for a complicated strategy game. One group wants rules that make the game useful for science projects. Another wants rules that fit the game’s own patterns and proofs. A third group wants both. If the groups disagree, they need more than a slogan such as “use the best method.” They must explain what counts as best, how much support is enough, and which group gets to decide.
summaries.summary: Naturalism in the philosophy of mathematics is a family of views about which standards should guide philosophical thinking about mathematics. Scientific naturalism looks to natural science. Mathematical naturalism looks to mathematics itself. Mathematical-cum-scientific naturalism gives a role to both. These views differ in strength. Some say a claim is acceptable only if the favored standards support it; others say those standards should simply have the greatest weight or should at least rule out incompatible claims. Naturalism is often anti-revisionist: it resists proposals to replace ordinary mathematics for reasons that do not come from mathematical or scientific practice. Still, mathematics has changed over time, so naturalists are not committed to never revising it. The entry examines several challenges. It may be unclear what counts as science, how scientific standards should be balanced, and whether the beliefs of scientists or mathematicians always reveal what their standards support. Naturalists are motivated by the success and agreement found in science and mathematics, but critics argue that success in one subject may not give authority over another. A special view, heterogeneous naturalism, separates mathematics proper from philosophy of mathematics. The entry also considers naturalism about what exists and the problem of explaining knowledge of abstract mathematical objects.
key_ideas: There are three main methodological versions: scientific, mathematical, and mathematical-cum-scientific naturalism.
Naturalism often opposes changing established mathematics because of an external philosophical theory, although it allows revisions that arise from mathematical or scientific practice.
Naturalists disagree about whether their standards must decide every issue, merely outweigh other standards, or only rule out conflicting claims.
It is hard to define one scientific method or draw a perfectly sharp line between mathematics and philosophy.
Arguments that science and mathematics are successful or widely agreed upon may support naturalism, but they may not prove that these fields should rule on philosophical questions.
Some naturalists argue that mathematical objects are physical or natural; this creates challenges involving abstractness, necessity, and our knowledge of mathematics.
summaries.why_it_matters: When people debate mathematics, they may be asking different questions: Which theorem follows from the rules? Which axioms should we choose? What do mathematical statements mean? Do numbers exist? Naturalism helps organize these questions and shows why a method that works for proving theorems may not automatically settle questions about mathematical reality. It also encourages careful thinking about evidence, authority, and disagreement.

important_terms.definition: The idea that philosophy of mathematics should give authority to science, mathematics, or both rather than to separate outside standards.
The standards mathematicians use, especially proof, consistency with accepted work, and productive mathematical practice.
The standards associated with scientific inquiry, such as evidence, explanation, simplicity, and successful prediction.
A naturalist view that gives mathematical standards priority for mathematics but scientific standards priority for philosophy of mathematics.
The difficulty of deciding exactly where science or mathematics ends and other activities begin.
The view that numbers and other mathematical objects exist independently of human thinkers, even though they are not physical objects.
A view that treats all existing things as natural, often meaning that everything is in space and time.

questions_to_think_about: Should philosophy ever reject a claim that mathematicians accept?
Does widespread agreement show that a method is reliable?
Why might a theory be successful in physics but not automatically authoritative about numbers?
Can a mathematical theory be true if it depends on which physical objects happen to exist?
Is it possible for mathematics to be influenced by philosophical ideas even if those ideas do not appear in formal proofs?
